Multiple imputation of a beta matrix

Source: vignettes/articles/multiple-imputation-beta.qmd 
library(slideimp)

pca_imp() and knn_imp() fill each missing value with one best guess. That is enough for many uses, but an analysis run on a singly imputed matrix treats the guesses as if they had been measured, so its standard errors come out too small. Multiple imputation instead draws several plausible values for every missing value, so the uncertainty about the missing cells carries through to the final estimate.

slideimp does this with a Bayesian low-rank (PCA) model, the method of Audigier, Husson and Josse (2016). This article goes through each step for a beta-value matrix (DNA methylation, values in [0, 1]), from tuning the model to a pooled estimate.

Simulate a beta matrix

The matrix below is built on the logit scale - a mean per CpG with the two modes typical of methylation, a rank-2 signal, and heavy-tailed noise - and then mapped into [0, 1] with plogis(). Half of the columns have 16 of their 80 samples set to NA.

This data follows the model the sampler assumes, so the fit will look good. It is here to show the steps, not to show how well the method works on real data.

set.seed(2)
n <- 80
p <- 300
mu <- ifelse(runif(p) < 0.5, rnorm(p, -2, 0.7), rnorm(p, 2, 0.7))
U <- matrix(rnorm(n * 2), n, 2)
V <- matrix(rnorm(p * 2, 0, 0.5), p, 2)
noise <- 0.4 * sqrt(4 / 6) * matrix(rt(n * p, df = 6), n, p)
truth <- plogis(matrix(mu, n, p, byrow = TRUE) + U %*% t(V) + noise)
dimnames(truth) <- list(sprintf("s%02d", seq_len(n)), sprintf("cpg%03d", seq_len(p)))

obj <- truth
na_cols <- sample.int(p, p / 2)
for (j in na_cols) obj[sample.int(n, 16), j] <- NA
obj[1:4, 1:4]
#>         cpg001    cpg002    cpg003     cpg004
#> s01 0.21050697 0.9090441 0.9077718 0.06148590
#> s02 0.13928224 0.7599630 0.7580556 0.07896476
#> s03 0.21884599 0.8688346 0.9009699 0.05805358
#> s04 0.04057579 0.8940313 0.7209590 0.09907192
mean(is.na(obj))
#> [1] 0.1

Row and column names are required: the fit uses them to keep track of which cell is which.

Tune the model with mipca_tune()

Two choices shape the model: the rank (how many components) and nu, the degrees of freedom of the noise. Inf gives Gaussian noise, and smaller values allow heavier tails.

mipca_tune() hides some observed cells, imputes them at each candidate rank, and scores the draws against the hidden truth with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS, lower is better). From the same draws it also estimates the nu that each rank implies, so one call informs both choices.

transform = "logit_biwhiten" is the transform for beta values. It maps the data onto the logit scale (after squeezing exact 0 and 1 inwards so the logit stays finite) and then rescales rows and columns. The sampler works on that scale, and every value it hands back is mapped back into [0, 1]. The argument has no default: pass transform = "identity" for data that is already roughly Gaussian.

tuned <- mipca_tune(
  obj,
  rank = 1:4,
  transform = "logit_biwhiten",
  seed = 1
)
tuned
#> si_tune: 4 ranks on a 80 x 300 matrix, holdout 200 cells over 50 columns
#>  rank    crps ess_p10 ess_ok rhat_max implied_nu implied_lo implied_hi  time
#>     1 0.04873   323.3 0.3365    1.032        Inf        Inf        Inf 0.167
#>     2 0.02606   305.4 0.2554    1.036      9.587      6.334        Inf 0.159
#>     3 0.02598   290.6 0.1992    1.039     13.679      4.561        Inf 0.241
#>     4 0.02618   277.6 0.1369    1.039      9.954      5.475        Inf 0.247
#>   next: mipca_fit(x, obj) fits the rank with the lowest crps.
#>         mipca_fit(x, obj, rank) fits another rank.

How to read the table:

  • crps: the mean score on the hidden cells. The best rank has the lowest crps.
  • ess_p10 and ess_ok: the 10th percentile of the effective sample size (ESS) over the values that Rhat and ESS are computed on, and the share of them with an ESS of at least 100 x chains (400 here, with the default 4 chains). Low values mean the chains are short, not that the rank is wrong. Run mipca_tune() again with a larger iter_sampling for longer chains.
  • rhat_max: the worst Rhat over the same values. Values well above 1.05 mean the chains disagree.
  • implied_nu, implied_lo and implied_hi: the noise degrees of freedom that the hidden cells imply at that rank, and its 68% bootstrap interval.
  • time: the seconds each rank took.

The table holds more columns than it prints. ?mipca_tune lists them all. The result column holds the score of each hidden cell, per rank:

head(tuned$result[[1]][, c("row", "col", "truth", "mean", "sd", "crps")])
#>   row col      truth       mean         sd       crps
#> 1   1   2 0.90904408 0.85357938 0.05664707 0.02975744
#> 2  15   2 0.89156589 0.92327401 0.05471297 0.02464390
#> 3  38   2 0.90441911 0.83230465 0.05491061 0.04333744
#> 4  60   2 0.90403138 0.89717857 0.05166960 0.01188086
#> 5  38  30 0.15984324 0.11436739 0.06370078 0.03423272
#> 6  40  30 0.08271408 0.04613398 0.04426940 0.02868168

Fit the model with mipca_fit()

mipca_fit(tuned, obj) runs the final fit at the rank with the lowest CRPS, with nu taken from that rank’s estimate and the chain settings carried over from the tuner. Pass the matrix again: the tuning table does not hold it. An implied nu below 5 is raised to 5, with a message, because the sampler can become unstable below 5. The transform is refitted on the full matrix.

fit <- mipca_fit(tuned, obj, seed = 2, refresh = 0)
fit
#> si_mi fit: 80 x 300, 2400 imputed cells, 400 draws
#>   next: as.matrix() with 'draw' for a completed matrix, summary() for Rhat and ESS

With the tuner’s default settings, this runs 4 chains with 100 warm-up and 100 sampling iterations each, so 400 draws are kept for every missing value.

To fit a rank and nu that do not come from a tuning table, call mipca() directly. mipca() also takes subset, which limits which columns have their draws stored. Every missing value is still drawn at every iteration, because the low-rank structure ties the columns together, so subset saves memory, not time. The stored draws take cells x draws of memory, so on a genome-scale matrix the saving is large.

Check convergence

summary() reports Rhat and ESS for a sample of the imputed cells.

summary(fit)
#> si_mi_summary: Rhat and ESS for 1200 cells in 150 columns
#>   prop_diag 0.5, 4 chains x 100 draws
#>           0% 25% 50%    75%   100%
#> rhat   0.992   1   1   1.01   1.04
#> ess  119.000 325 360 393.00 536.00
#> worst 6 cells by rhat:
#>  chunk col   name row     rhat      ess
#>      1 137 cpg137  11 1.040830 118.6063
#>      1 120 cpg120  58 1.029801 220.7080
#>      1  59 cpg059  38 1.027809 200.7972
#>      1 118 cpg118  41 1.025974 213.3689
#>      1 113 cpg113  12 1.024725 156.2937
#>      1 236 cpg236  34 1.024028 154.6561

The five numbers for each row are the minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile and maximum across cells. Most cells here have Rhat near 1 and an ESS in the hundreds, so the chains agree and the 400 draws are worth a few hundred independent ones. The cells with the highest Rhat are listed below the summary. If many of them sit above an Rhat of 1.05, or the ESS is low, run longer chains, for example with mipca_fit(tuned, obj, iter_sampling = 400).

Extract completed matrices

as.matrix(fit, draw = b) returns one completed matrix: the observed values, with draw b filled into the missing values. The rest of this article follows two CpGs with missing values.

two <- names(sort(colSums(is.na(obj)), decreasing = TRUE))[1:2]
completed_1 <- as.matrix(fit, draw = 1)
dim(completed_1)
#> [1]  80 300
head(completed_1[, two])
#>         cpg001    cpg005
#> s01 0.21050697 0.9605862
#> s02 0.13928224 0.9314553
#> s03 0.21884599 0.9629385
#> s04 0.04057579 0.8823267
#> s05 0.18268468 0.9643872
#> s06 0.21027450 0.9652667

Completed matrices are built one at a time, so the draws are never all expanded into memory at once. Each one is a full copy of obj, so keep only what the analysis needs. A typical analysis takes a few dozen draws spread across the chains. The draws are numbered chain by chain, so evenly spaced numbers take some from every chain. This example takes 20:

draws <- round(seq(1, 400, length.out = 20)) # print(fit) shows 400 draws
completed <- lapply(draws, function(b) as.matrix(fit, draw = b)[, two])
length(completed)
#> [1] 20

Each missing value now has a distribution rather than a single value. For one missing cell, here are its 20 draws next to its true value in truth:

miss_row <- which(is.na(obj[, two[1]]))[1]
cell_draws <- vapply(completed, function(m) m[miss_row, two[1]], numeric(1))
quantile(cell_draws, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
#>        5%       50%       95% 
#> 0.1500064 0.2038251 0.3122086
truth[miss_row, two[1]]
#> [1] 0.2257819

Pool an estimate

Run the analysis on every completed matrix and combine the results with Rubin’s rules. As an example, estimate the mean beta value of the first of the two CpGs:

est <- vapply(completed, function(m) mean(m[, two[1]]), numeric(1))
within <- vapply(completed, function(m) var(m[, two[1]]) / nrow(m), numeric(1))

M <- length(completed)
q_bar <- mean(est) # pooled estimate
w <- mean(within) # average within-imputation variance
b <- var(est) # between-imputation variance
total <- w + (1 + 1 / M) * b # total variance

c(estimate = q_bar, se = sqrt(total), se_single = sqrt(w))
#>   estimate         se  se_single 
#> 0.23271605 0.02261688 0.02231940
mean(truth[, two[1]])
#> [1] 0.2357462

se_single is the standard error you would report from one completed matrix. The pooled se adds the between-imputation variance b, which is the uncertainty about the missing cells that single imputation leaves out. Here only 16 of 80 values are missing and the model fits well, so the difference is small. It grows with the share of missing values.

Columns near 0 or 1: abb

Some CpGs are almost always unmethylated or almost always methylated, so nearly all of their observed values sit at or next to 0 or 1. abb_cols() returns the column numbers of such columns. Passed as abb, they are left out of the model, and their missing values are drawn from their own observed values by approximate Bayesian bootstrap. This keeps the exact 0s and 1s such columns often hold, but it does not keep their relation to the other columns.

The simulated matrix has no such column:

abb_cols(obj)
#> integer(0)

Move the first of the two CpGs towards 0 and the second towards 1, and abb_cols() returns both:

obj_abb <- obj
obj_abb[, two[1]] <- obj_abb[, two[1]] / 100
obj_abb[, two[2]] <- 1 - (1 - obj_abb[, two[2]]) / 100
abb <- abb_cols(obj_abb)
colnames(obj_abb)[abb]
#> [1] "cpg001" "cpg005"

Pass them to mipca_tune() as abb. It leaves the abb columns out of tuning, and mipca_fit() reads abb from the table. Every draw for an abb column is one of that column’s observed values:

tuned_abb <- mipca_tune(
  obj_abb,
  rank = 1:4,
  transform = "logit_biwhiten",
  seed = 1,
  abb = abb
)
fit_abb <- mipca_fit(tuned_abb, obj_abb, seed = 2, refresh = 0)

miss <- is.na(obj_abb[, two[1]])
drawn <- as.matrix(fit_abb, draw = 1)[miss, two[1]]
all(drawn %in% obj_abb[!miss, two[1]])
#> [1] TRUE

Impute target CpGs on flanking windows

When only some CpGs need draws, such as the CpGs of an epigenetic clock, each one can be fitted on the CpGs near it instead of on the whole matrix. mipca_flank_plan() finds the window of each target: the columns within window_size of it on location, on both sides. A target whose window has fewer than min_window_n columns is not imputed. mipca_flank() then fits mipca() on each window and keeps the target’s draws.

The simulated CpGs have no genomic positions, so the column order stands in for them here. Use real coordinates, one chromosome at a time, on real data.

location <- seq_len(ncol(obj))
plan <- mipca_flank_plan(
  obj,
  location,
  window_size = 20,
  subset = two,
  min_window_n = 10
)
plan
#> si_flank_plan: 2 targets on a 80 x 300 matrix, nothing fitted
#>   status: impute 2
#>  target   name n_miss start end window_n status
#>       1 cpg001     16     1  21       21 impute
#>       5 cpg005     16     1  25       25 impute
#>   next: mipca_flank(x, rank, seed, transform) imputes.
#>         mipca_flank_window(x, subset) gives one target's window to tune on.

To choose the rank and nu for the windows, tune on one target’s window. A window has few columns, so lower n_cols, the number of columns that get hidden cells. Its default is 10% of the columns, but at least 50:

win <- mipca_flank_window(plan, two[1])
tuned_win <- mipca_tune(
  win,
  rank = 1:3,
  transform = "logit_biwhiten",
  n_cols = 10,
  seed = 1
)
tuned_win
#> si_tune: 3 ranks on a 80 x 21 matrix, holdout 40 cells over 10 columns
#>  rank    crps ess_p10 ess_ok rhat_max implied_nu implied_lo implied_hi  time
#>     1 0.04828   278.1  0.095    1.030      3.045      2.620      10.98 0.026
#>     2 0.03778   233.7  0.040    1.045        Inf      8.555        Inf 0.026
#>     3 0.03835   193.1  0.015    1.054        Inf        Inf        Inf 0.042
#>   next: mipca_fit(x, obj) fits the rank with the lowest crps.
#>         mipca_fit(x, obj, rank) fits another rank.

Then give the rank and nu to mipca_flank(). It warns about a nu below 5 but does not raise it, so raise it to 5 here, as mipca_fit() would:

best <- which.min(tuned_win$crps)
fit_flank <- mipca_flank(
  plan,
  rank = tuned_win$rank[best],
  nu = max(tuned_win$implied_nu[best], 5),
  seed = 1,
  transform = "logit_biwhiten",
  .progress = FALSE
)
fit_flank
#> si_mi fit: 80 x 2, 32 imputed cells, 400 draws
#>   next: as.matrix() with 'draw' for a completed matrix, summary() for Rhat and ESS
dim(as.matrix(fit_flank, draw = 1))
#> [1] 80  2

The fit holds the targets only, and as.matrix(), summary() and the pooling above work on it as on a fit from mipca(). cbind() joins the fits of several matrices, such as one per chromosome.

Reference

Audigier, V., Husson, F. and Josse, J. (2016). Multiple imputation for continuous variables using a Bayesian principal component analysis. Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation, 86(11), 2140-2156. https://doi.org/10.1080/00949655.2015.1104683
